\chapter{And, Or, and Neither}
\label{ch:pa-and-or-neither}
\hlchaptermodality{38}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can join two things or two whole sentences with ate, offer a choice with jaan, and refuse both halves at once with na ... na.}

The coordinators, and the first two-clause sentence this book can make -- until now the longest structure the track taught was a single clause of four slots. ate has a shorter twin, te, which is also a syllable the script lessons drill, which is exactly why a search of the corpus for and kept finding the drill and never the conjunction. na ... na is the first joining pattern in the book that stands in FRONT of both halves rather than between them.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ate]{\pa{ਅਤੇ} (ate) — and}

\label{lesson:PA-C38-ate}



\begin{quote}
From the chapter behind you, the two admissions. And from the food chapter far back, the word for \textbf{milk}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{mainū̃ samajh nahī̃ āī}, \emph{mainū̃ nahī̃ patā} — then \emph{dudh}
\end{itemize}

Milk and bread were taught together, and read back together at a distant window. Until this lesson there has been no way to name them in one breath.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਦੁੱਧ} \pa{ਅਤੇ} \pa{ਰੋਟੀ}} — \emph{dudh ate roṭī} — \textbf{milk and bread}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}} stands between the two things it joins, exactly where English puts \emph{and}.

It has a shorter twin. In ordinary speech Punjabi very often says just \textbf{\pa{ਤੇ}}, and the two are the same word — \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}} is the fuller, more written form. That matters here for an odd reason: the short \textbf{\pa{ਤੇ}} is also a syllable this book drills in its script lessons, so a search of the corpus for \emph{and} kept finding the drill and never the conjunction. The word looked present and was absent.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dudh ate roṭī}.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dudh} alone, then the pair. Hear what the middle word buys.
  \item \emph{Build:} any two things you can name, joined.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Join two foods. What is the shorter everyday form of \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}}, and why did it make the word hard to find in this book? (\textbf{\pa{ਤੇ}} — it is also a script drill syllable.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[… ate …]{\pa{ਅਤੇ}, joining two sentences}

\label{lesson:PA-C38-ate-vaak}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, the joining word. Four lessons back, at the head of the last chapter, where \textbf{\pa{ਨਹੀਂ}} stands.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{ate}, and \emph{nahī̃} before the verb
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The same \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}} joins two whole sentences, and changes nothing about either:

\begin{quote}
\emph{(first sentence)} \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}} \emph{(second sentence)}
\end{quote}

No ending appears, no word moves. That is why \emph{and} is the joining word to learn first: it is the only one that costs the sentences on either side of it nothing at all.

And it composes with the chapter behind you — the second half is free to be a negative:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{… \pa{ਅਤੇ} … \pa{ਨਹੀਂ} …}
\end{quote}

That is a two-clause sentence, and it is the first one this book has been able to make. Until now the longest thing the track taught was a single clause of four slots.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Build:} two short sentences you own, joined with \emph{ate}.
  \item \emph{Build:} the same again, the second half negative.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} the two said separately, then joined. Same words.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What changes about a sentence when \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}} joins it to another? (Nothing.) Make one whose second half is negative.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ate]{\pa{ਅਤੇ} reaches the page}

\label{lesson:PA-C38-ate-write}



\begin{quote}
One chapter back you wrote \textbf{\pa{ਨਹੀਂ}}. Write it once from memory, bindi and all, before anything is uncovered.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — three pieces, none new}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਅ}} — the vowel carrier · \textbf{\pa{ਤ}} — \emph{ta} · \textbf{\pa{ੇ}} — the laav stroke above
\end{quote}

All three were taught long before this chapter. Say it plainly: the word this book most needed was never a writing problem. Nobody had written it down.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, model in view}
Keep the model in view and copy \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}} once. Check the laav sits above \textbf{\pa{ਤ}}, not above \textbf{\pa{ਅ}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Write \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}} from memory. How many of its three signs were new today? (None.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jāṁ]{\pa{ਜਾਂ} (jāṁ) — or}

\label{lesson:PA-C38-jaan}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back you wrote the joining word. Say it, then write it in the air.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}} offers you both. \textbf{\pa{ਜਾਂ}} offers you one of two:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਦੁੱਧ} \pa{ਜਾਂ} \pa{ਰੋਟੀ}} — \emph{dudh jāṁ roṭī} — \textbf{milk or bread}
\end{quote}

Same position, different job: it stands between the two things and asks the listener to choose. The bindi on it is not decoration — the vowel goes through the nose, and this book has been marking that since its earliest script lessons.

This is the word a shopkeeper uses on you, and the one you need to answer with.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dudh jāṁ roṭī}, then \emph{dudh ate roṭī}. One asks, one gives.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} the two joining words back to back, twice.
  \item \emph{Build:} offer someone a choice of two things you can name.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Offer a choice, then offer both. Which word did each need? (\emph{jāṁ} to choose, \emph{ate} to give both.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nā … nā …]{\pa{ਨਾ} … \pa{ਨਾ} … (nā … nā …) — neither … nor}

\label{lesson:PA-C38-na-na}



\begin{quote}
The two joining words of this chapter, and the rule from the chapter before it.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{ate}, \emph{jāṁ} — and \emph{nahī̃} before the verb
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
English uses two different words — \emph{neither} and \emph{nor}. Punjabi repeats \textbf{one}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਨਾ}} \emph{(first thing)} \textbf{\pa{ਨਾ}} \emph{(second thing)} — \textquotedblleft{}neither … nor …\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\pa{ਨਾ}} is the short bare negative you have already met beside \textbf{\pa{ਨਹੀਂ}}. Here it does the joining and the negating at once, standing in front of \textbf{each} item rather than between them.

That is worth noticing against \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}} and \textbf{\pa{ਜਾਂ}}, which stand \textbf{between}. This is the first joining pattern in the book that goes in front of both halves.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} refuse two things at once with \emph{nā … nā …}.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{ate} between, then \emph{nā … nā} in front of each.
  \item \emph{Run through:} offered a choice with \emph{jāṁ}, refuse both.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Refuse two things in one sentence. Where does \textbf{\pa{ਨਾ}} stand, and how is that different from \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}}? (In front of each item; \emph{ate} stands between them.) Next chapter: \textbf{but} — and Punjabi has two words for it, one from each side of the language's history.
\end{tcolorbox}
